problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}$ that lies between the lines $y=0$ and $y=\sqrt[4]{3}.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}) \\  & ={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}={y}^{4}.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{y}^{4}.$ Then, ${y}^{3}\text{d}y=(\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{3}}{y}^{3}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[\frac{2(4)^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$
